rule: mixed: 'Summer hunting' is taken as one particular hunting rather than hunting in general, so the sentence is recorded as a single episode instead of the standing regularity and nothing can fire on it. Make the subject a plain plural so it reads as a claim about every such hunt: "Summer hunts yield the autumn feather store."
texts: mixed: the conditional itself does come out as one fireable rule, but 'often' has nowhere to sit inside the condition — it is spent on the rule's own reliability (the rule is recorded as holding only about 80% of the time) and is separately asserted as the standing fact that sky-cats hunt often, which the sentence only supposes. Split the frequency into its own claim and leave the condition plain: "Sky-cats hunt often through summer. When sky-cats hunt through summer, many feathers accumulate at the cliff base by autumn."

bad: the rule can never fire — the hunting in the 'if' clause is written as a per-cat term that no real hunting event can ever match — and 'often' is again both spent on the rule's reliability and asserted outright as fact. Use the 'when' wording, which does produce a matchable condition, and move the frequency into its own sentence: "Sky-cats hunt often in summer. When sky-cats hunt in summer, the autumn feather store grows."

mixed: the causing and both activities are recorded, but 'frequent hunting' and 'frequent molting' each become one particular thing, so the sentence reads as a single episode of one hunting causing one molting rather than a general law, and nothing can fire on it. State the covariation with finite clauses and an explicit subject: "The more often sky-cats hunt, the more often they molt."
